Supporting libraries and books after the midterms
Midterm elections brought sweeping change across the country. New leadership brings with it incredible opportunity for library champions and freedom to read advocates to build upon that change.
Advocacy is brimming with opportunity right now.

Though Florida’s midterm outcomes weren’t what folks hoped for, there’s still tremendous space for good work to be done. There are challenges, including the possibility of seeing public libraries decimated through the passage of Amendment 3, but nothing is a done deal yet.

Residents of newly blue states have the chance to help mitigate the damage done by cruel legislation targeting libraries, books, and librarians/educators caught in the crosshairs. This is the moment for amplifying demands to protect these institutions.

There are still four book ban proposals on Capitol Hill, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services still has no budget for Fiscal Year 2027. Get on the phone with current and incoming lawmakers and make it clear what’s expected of them.

Many states will see more elections in the spring for school and library board seats. Gear up to help friends, family, and neighbors navigate these crucial local elections, and consider running for a seat if you’re able.
Get a host of ideas and discover resources to help you roll up your sleeves on literary advocacy after the 2026 Midterms here. – KJ

2026 has been a great year for graphic novel adaptations. From modern classics to a cozy fantasy sensation, fresh artwork and storytelling enhances these familiar stories and introduces them to a brand new audience.
Here are four books that got the graphic novel treatment in 2026.

The Midnight Library: The Graphic Novel by Matt Haig, Adapted and Illustrated by Fred Fordham – Matt Haig’s blockbuster bestseller about a magical library whose books contain every possible version of a person’s life, with each of Nora’s lives rendered in vivid, immersive illustrations.

A Confederacy of Dunces: A Graphic Novel Adaptation by John Kennedy Toole, Written and Illustrated by Albert Monteys* – Set in New Orleans’ French Quarter, this Pulitzer Prize–winning cult classic satirizing 1960s America gets a whole new life with this graphic treatment.

Legends & Lattes: The Graphic Novel by Travis Baldree, Adapted by Samuel Sattin, Illustrated by Shanti Rittgers and Sarah Webb – The coziest of fantasies gets even more cozy with dreamy illustrations, and a little more romance than the original.

In the Time of the Butterflies: The Graphic Novel by Julia Alvarez, Adapted and Illustrated by Krystal Quiles – A gorgeous new version of a modern classic from one of our most important Latine authors, where three brave sisters fight against the Trujillo dictatorship.
Across Turtle Island, Indigenous horror is doing something truly spectacular.
These authors tackle themes like ancestral and inherited grief and resilience in the face of the horrors of ongoing colonial violence.
Their stories are well-crafted gems, terrifying in the best way.
Combine them with a talented narrator, and you have a thrilling audiobook perfect for autumn listening.
Here are a few to get you started:

Bad Cree by Jessica Johns, narrated by Tanis Parenteau: Tanis Parenteau brilliantly performs this debut novel that is one part horror and one part family story. Her voice allows the horror to creep up on the listener. I was terrified in the best way possible.

The Buffalo Hunter Hunter by Stephen Graham Jones, narrated by Shane Ghostkeeper, Marin Ireland, Owen Teale: This novel is one of the best vampire stories ever told. Shane Ghostkeeper’s tone and emotional depth of his narration mark him as a talent to watch.

And Then She Fell by Alicia Elliot, narrated by Cheri Maracle and Jenna Clause: Cheri Maracle and Jenna Clause’s narration teases out each unique feature in the protagonists’ voices. If you pick this up, be prepared to be on the edge of your seat the whole way through.
Learn more about these Indigenous horror audiobooks. —KW
An excerpt from LeVar Burton’s new memoir

LeVar Burton is the iconic actor behind roles like Kunta Kinte in Roots and Geordi LaForge in Star Trek: The Next Generation. He was also the host of Reading Rainbow. Below is an excerpt from his memoir, Take My Word for It, out now from Random House.

If you take Roots, Reading Rainbow, Star Trek, all those pieces together, what you get is my Work. But I’m not necessarily talking about the specifics of the characters I played, although I’m sure that’s part of it. I’m talking about the aggregate of it all—what those roles represent in the grand scheme of life.

It is now my understanding that show business has only been my entry point into a broader work. Reading Rainbow gave me the credibility to champion the cause of literacy worldwide and to speak out against the scourge of book bans. It created a legacy that will likely outlive me; at least I hope so. Roots provided me with a platform to discuss racism in America and how Black people have constantly had to navigate life with a hypervigilance that affects every aspect of our lives, health, and communities. Star Trek gave me the authority to address the future of humanity and emphasize how we heal ourselves from the illusion that race, color, creed, and national boundaries are legitimate reasons for conflict. Speaking about my rage à la James Baldwin in the miniseries Clipped opened the door for me to discuss that which lies beneath the surface of most Black people in America. All of this is part of the Work I believe I’ve been sent here to do. The roles were simply vehicles; they are the mechanisms through which the Work is revealed. In short, it’s why I’m here on this planet—what my soul agreed to do when I took this body.

And as I look at my personal evolution alongside my career trajectory, one thing stands out: from Kunta to the Reading Rainbow guy to Geordi, I’ve been blessed to represent a continuum of the Black experience in America, moving from our enslavement, through the present, and on to a star-faring future. For some, that might feel like a heavy thing to carry. But the wild thing is, to me it doesn’t feel like a weight at all. It feels like a privilege. Because, really, who gets to do that? To have grown up in a country where three generations ago it would’ve been illegal for me to know how to read and now be a symbol of literacy? Come on! This lifetime was planned.

Speaking of Netflix adaptations, there are many great ones that are either birthed from YA novels or that reimagine stories with younger protagonists.
The following adaptations are all on Netflix. In them, love gets messy, one bullied teen in Brazil gets a summer he’ll never forget, and a sword-toting princess avenges her father.

To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before: It feels like this adaptation of the 2014 bestselling release by Jenny Han came at a time when the Netflix adaptation game wasn’t as strong. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if the success of this movie encouraged more YA adaptations.

The 2018 release follows the book fairly closely, though there are also a few differences. High schooler Lara Jean’s world gets rocked when the love letters she wrote to her five crushes get mailed out to them.

Here the Whole Time: This Brazilian-set coming-of-age film was adapted from a 2017 YA novel of the same name in English, but originally titled Quinze Dias by Vitor Martins, translated by Larissa Helena.

Interestingly enough, the novel gets compared to To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before, except the main character is a fat gay teenager who finds out his crush is staying with him and his mother for 15 days one summer.
Scarlet: This fantastical anime adaptation of Shakespeare’s Hamlet looks gorgeous. It follows a teen princess on a quest to avenge her father. —EE
